Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette:
Six months ago, Kenji was a man who took pride in his predictability. At 63, his life as a financial analyst in the city was a well-ordered landscape of spreadsheets, client meetings, and the quiet comfort of his 35-year marriage. That order was shattered on a rainy Tuesday night in November. Driving home late, he’d entered an intersection on a green light, only to be T-boned by a speeding sedan that ran the red. The world became a deafening screech of tires, the sickening crunch of metal, and then a profound, suffocating darkness. Trapped in the driver's seat with the smell of gasoline stinging his nostrils, he could only listen to the hiss of the ruined engine as he waited for help to arrive.

In the weeks that followed, the accident began to replay itself in fragments, ambushing him without warning. The sound of a truck's air brakes outside his office window would instantly bring back the memory, not as a recollection, but as a visceral, present-tense event. He would hear the shriek of tires in his own head, feeling the phantom jolt of the impact as if it were happening all over again. Because the memory returned with such sensory force, he began to see and hear echoes of it everywhere; the suffocating darkness of the crash was now in every unlit room, and the shriek of tires was latent in the sound of any passing car. Each sudden sound told him, with an unshakable certainty, that his prior sense of order had been a foolish illusion and that the world was, in fact, a place of random, brutal danger. These sensory intrusions felt so real that his body would react before his mind could catch up; his heart would hammer against his ribs, and a cold sweat would break out across his skin. He found himself scanning the exits of his own office building, a place he had worked for two decades, his body convinced that imminent danger required an escape route. This constant state of high alert seemed to prime his mind for the memory; on days when he felt most on edge, the intrusive images and sounds of the crash were hardest to keep at bay.

Kenji soon came to believe that the world was an fundamentally unsafe place and that he had been naive to think otherwise. This conviction, that he had to be on guard at all times, became the organising principle of his life. This belief that he had foolishly misjudged the world’s dangers kept his mind circling back to the accident itself, searching the memory for the mistake he must have made or the warning sign he’d missed. The belief that you never know what can happen next meant he could no longer tolerate darkness; he began leaving lights on all over the house, and the thought of entering the underground parking garage at work was enough to make him feel short of breath. This constant vigilance made him hyper-attuned to the very sounds and smells that haunted him. Every car horn, every whiff of exhaust on the street, became a potential harbinger of disaster, confirming his need to be perpetually careful and pulling his attention back to the possibility of threat. Each time he flinched at a sound, it served as fresh proof for his new conviction: the world was treacherous, and his previous sense of safety had been a dangerous illusion.

This cycle of fear has become a tightening loop. His core belief that he must remain vigilant fuels his threat-monitoring behaviours; he wakes several times a night, listening for any sound, his body rigid with tension until he can confirm the house is secure. The persistent state of high alert makes him exquisitely sensitive to triggers, so that even the distant sound of a siren can feel like a direct threat. When a memory does break through—triggered by a car backfiring or the sudden darkness of a power flicker—it arrives with the full force of the original trauma. The auditory recall of the crash floods his senses, and the feeling of being trapped returns. This vivid re-experiencing launches an immediate, powerful threat response; his body reacts to the memory as if it were a present danger, which in turn reinforces the intrusive power of the memory itself. He is caught in a feedback loop where the memory fuels the sense of threat, and the threat makes the memory feel more immediate and harder to escape.

His world has shrunk dramatically. He has not driven since the accident, forcing his wife to chauffeur him everywhere, a dependency he finds deeply shameful. The final straw came last week when a car alarm went off in a shopping mall parking lot. The sudden, loud noise sent him into a full-blown panic. He dropped his shopping bags and crouched between two cars, convinced he was about to be hit. His wife found him trembling, unable to speak. It was her tearful plea that evening that finally brought him to therapy. He feels he is losing his mind, trapped in a constant state of alarm, and is terrified that the calm, predictable man he once was is gone for good.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not describe how external triggers cause or reinforce the patient's negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not explain how the patient's negative appraisals cause the trauma memory to intrude.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not describe how re-experiencing the trauma memory leads to an increased sensitivity to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
